sources.source: GDPR Article 5 — Principles relating to processing of personal data

items.item: Personal data must be kept, in identifiable form, no longer than the purpose for which it's processed requires ('storage limitation').

at.step: Reveal: the law names the clock

sources.source: GDPR Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default

items.item: Protective measures must be designed in at the time of determining the means of processing, not retrofitted afterward.

items.item: Storage period and accessibility are named explicitly among what must default to the minimum necessary.

at.deep: Production failures this topic warns about

items.item: A dataset is either a system of record (the one authoritative copy) or a derived store (rebuildable from it) — that distinction decides what needs careful backup.

at.step: Reveal: system of record versus derived stores

items.item: The dominant access path (the one query shape accounting for most of the cost) picks the partition key, not an intuition about what sounds fast.

at.step: Reveal: the dominant access path picks the partition key

items.item: A table format is chosen by the same access-path reasoning, with interoperability and catalog consequences as the one decisive cost between otherwise similar formats.

at.step: Reveal: a table format, picked by its one decisive cost

items.item: The same query drawn as a band across two layouts makes the pruned-versus-touched fraction a measurable, not abstract, consequence of the partition key chosen.

at.step: Reveal: the same query, drawn as a band across two layouts

items.item: A retention tier is a retention period attached to a class of data, not merely a cheaper place to store old files.

at.step: Reveal: hot, warm and cold tiers, each with its own clock

items.item: The partition key that makes a query cheap can make erasure expensive: a key that scatters one subject's rows (date, here) forces a deletion request to touch every shelf the layout has.

items.item: Erasure designed in from the start costs choosing a key strategy up front; retrofitted onto an existing layout, it costs rewriting every shelf that subject's data ever touched.

at.deep: Production failures this topic warns about

items.item: This topic leaves out table-format internals (Chapter 6) and partition-pruning mechanics (Chapter 2 §2.4) deliberately — it teaches the decision those mechanics execute, not the mechanics themselves.

A point-lookup access path (session id) still needs the same two-part check as a date-range path: does the partition key match the dominant query, and does that same key group one subject's data together.
This topic fixes the shop's own system-of-record and access-path reasoning that the next topic (processing and serving choices) reads the resulting layout against.
